title: API
content:
A game typically subclasses DirectorBrain, swaps the action list, and calls the three Ticks from its own loop.

Achieve.Tempo.World

WorldReaction

Member	Signature	Description
ActiveEvents	IReadOnlyList<ReactionEvent>	List of live events
BurningCells	int	Currently burning cell count
ApplyElement	(Vector3 pos, float radius, ElementTag e, float power)	Stamp an element over an area
SetWind	(Vector2 dir, float strength)	Set the wind
Fill / SetCell	(string material) / (int x, int y, string material)	Lay down the grid
GetCell	(int x, int y) → ElementalState	Read a cell's state
Tick	(float dt)	Spread + refresh the list

Value types

ElementalState (struct) — MaterialId, Temperature, Wetness, Charge, OnFire, Frozen

ReactionEvent (struct) — Position, Magnitude, Ttl, Kind

MaterialDef — Name, Flammability, Conductivity, IgnitionPoint, FreezePoint, WaterAbsorption

ReactionRule — Trigger, TargetMaterials(;), Effect, Probability, Threshold, TargetMaterialList, MatchesMaterial, static Split

enum ElementTag — None, Fire, Water, Ice, Electric, Wind

enum StateEffect — Ignite, Extinguish, Wet, Dry, Freeze, Thaw, Charge, Discharge

Achieve.Tempo.Director

DirectorBrain (abstract)

Member	Signature	Description
CurrentPhase	Phase	The current phase
Tick	(WorldReaction, TensionModel, Vector3 playerPos, float dt)	Pick a phase and seed conditions
ActionPool	virtual IReadOnlyList<SeedAction>	The action list (override)
PickActions	virtual IEnumerable<SeedAction>	Action-selection policy (override)
MaxActiveEvents	virtual int	Simultaneous-event cap

DefaultDirectorBrain — default implementation to use without overrides.

SeedAction (abstract) — Cost, Intent, CanSeed, Seed.

Built-in actions: DryUpwind, IgniteUpwind, ChargeStorm, SummonRain.

enum SeedIntent — Prepare, Trigger, Calm.

enum Phase — BuildUp, Peak, Relax.

PhaseFsm — Evaluate(float tension, float dt) → Phase, Current, Reset().

Achieve.Tempo.Tension

TensionModel

Member	Signature	Description
Current	float	Tension the director reads, 0–1
PlayerStress	float	Player stress, 0–1
OnPlayerDamaged	(float dmg, float maxHp)	Immediate spike on hit
Tick	(Vector3 playerPos, WorldReaction, float dt)	Update tension
SampleThreat	protected virtual (Vector3) → float	Threat signal (swappable)
SampleAround	protected virtual (Vector3, WorldReaction) → float	Nearby signal (swappable)

Achieve.Tempo.Config

DataService<T> — GetDataCenter(), Register(T), Reset().

TensionConfig — strengths, radii, weights, speeds, thresholds.

PhaseData — PeakEnter/RelaxEnter/BuildUpEnter/MinRelax, per-phase budgets, BudgetFor(Phase).

ActionData — Actions, Add(SeedAction).

RuleData — Materials, Rules, ResolveMaterialId, GetMaterial, AddMaterial, AddRule, spread thresholds.

Achieve.Tempo.Editor

RuleValidator — Validate(RuleData) → List<Issue>, menu Tools/Tempo/Validate Rules, automatic pre-build check.

DebugWindow — Bind(TensionModel, DirectorBrain, WorldReaction), menu Tools/Tempo/Debug Window.

1.0.0 — 2026-06-27

Added

World reaction (Achieve.Tempo.World): WorldReaction spreading fire/water/ice/electricity by
rules on a flat grid, per-cell ElementalState, MaterialDef, table-driven ReactionRule
(single-field ; input), and the live-event ReactionEvent.

Director (Achieve.Tempo.Director): DirectorBrain with a default policy extended via virtual,
the SeedAction seeding action plus four built-ins (DryUpwind/IgniteUpwind/ChargeStorm/SummonRain),
and PhaseFsm phase switching (hysteresis).

Tension (Achieve.Tempo.Tension): TensionModel combining two signals into 0–1 (rise fast, fall slow).

Config (Achieve.Tempo.Config): the code-separated data center DataService<T> and
TensionConfig/PhaseData/ActionData/RuleData (with defaults).

Editor tools (Achieve.Tempo.Editor): RuleValidator (pre-build rule-table check) and
DebugWindow (live tension/phase view).

Tests: EditMode (TensionModel/PhaseFsm/ReactionRule/RuleValidator),
PlayMode (spread direction, quench, event cleanup).

title: Match-3 puzzle
content:
Why it fits: the ReactionRule table is exactly the "what happens when special tiles meet" table.
"Water quenches fire" just becomes "rocket + bomb = mega-blast" — same structure.

Mapping the parts

Tempo	In a match-3
WorldReaction grid	The puzzle board (cascade = grid spread)
ReactionRule	Special-tile combo table: Trigger=special tile, Target=neighbor tile kinds, Effect=clear/convert
DataService<RuleData>	Swap the table to add new special tiles = live-ops without a code change
TensionModel	Player pressure (moves left, objective progress) → difficulty rubber-banding
DirectorBrain phases	Easy start (BuildUp) → endgame clutch (Peak) → calm after clear (Relax)
SeedAction	DropGoodPiece (a nudge when stuck) · AddBlocker (when too easy)

Rule-table example

Change only the element and it becomes a match-3 combo table.

// "A rocket clears nearby tiles of 3 kinds, in a line"
new ReactionRule {
    Trigger = ElementTag.Fire,             // = Rocket
    TargetMaterials = "Red;Blue;Green",    // neighbor tile kinds (one field, ;-separated)
    Effect = StateEffect.Extinguish,       // = Clear
    Probability = 1f,
};

RuleValidator catches "unknown tile kind / conflicting rules" before the build, so growing the table
during live-ops stays safe.

Rubber-banding with the director

The heart of match-3 is the "barely cleared it" feeling. The director watches tension (move-count
pressure) and seeds conditions — drop a good piece when stuck (DropGoodPiece), add a blocker when it's
too easy. But telegraph (the next-piece preview) so it reads as "see and decide," not "luck."

Mobile checkpoints

The table is live content. Add a new event tile as one RuleData row, ship it via remote data with no app update.

Rubber-band subtly. Too blatant and players notice. Ease it with RiseSpeed/FallSpeed.

Cascades thrilling, caps clear. A concurrent-cascade cap prevents stutter on low-end devices.

title: Survivor-like
content:
Why it fits: this genre is essentially Left 4 Dead's "AI Director" by another name. Tempo's
tension → director → world loop is the swarm ↔ breather rhythm.

Mapping the parts

Tempo	In a survivor-like
TensionModel.Current	Enemy spawn density / difficulty gauge
SampleThreat	On-screen enemy count + boss proximity
SampleAround	Ground-hazard (poison/fire/electric field) danger
DirectorBrain phases	Lull (BuildUp) → rush/elite (Peak) → breather (Relax)
SeedAction	SpawnSwarm · SpawnElite · OpenHazardZone · DropHealing
WorldReaction	Fire seas / poison clouds spreading on the grid (as-is)
Safeguard caps	Max simultaneous enemies/hazards = mobile heat / battery / frame defense

The flow

In build-up you thin enemies and let healing/items trickle in for a breather; once tension settles low,
a rush is coming. In peak you open an elite wave plus ground hazards at once to squeeze the screen. But
you must telegraph first (wave warning ring, ground glowing red) so it never feels like a cheap death.

public sealed class SurvivorDirector : DirectorBrain
{
    protected override IReadOnlyList<SeedAction> ActionPool => _actions;
    protected override int MaxActiveEvents => 60; // mobile: cap concurrent danger to fight heat

    // Threat from on-screen enemy count and boss proximity.
    public sealed class WaveTension : TensionModel
    {
        public int OnScreenEnemies; public float BossProximity;
        protected override float SampleThreat(Vector3 p)
            => Mathf.Clamp01(OnScreenEnemies / 40f) * 0.7f + BossProximity * 0.3f;
    }
}

SpawnSwarm/SpawnElite don't spawn enemies directly — they seed spawn conditions (open a spawn
gate); your game's pooling/placement picks them up. The director only decides when and how much.

Mobile checkpoints

Caps are your perf budget. MaxActiveEvents and a concurrent-enemy cap protect frames on low-end devices.

Sessions are short. Keep phase cycles around 1–2 minutes so build-up → peak → relax loops several times per run.

Telegraph big. On a small screen warnings get lost; make them obvious with rings / screen-edge reddening.

title: Tower defense
content:
Why it fits: two things click at once — the director's wave pacing (Left 4 Dead) and freeze/shock
chaining through enemy crowds (BotW's electric chain, verbatim).

Mapping the parts

Tempo	In a tower defense
TensionModel	Defense-line pressure (leaked enemies, core HP)
DirectorBrain phases	Scout (BuildUp) → rush/special mob (Peak) → regroup (Relax)
SeedAction	SeedColdSnap (freeze field) · ChargeStorm (shock chain) · SpawnRusher
WorldReaction	Status propagation: freeze/shock jumps from an afflicted enemy to neighbors (elemental reaction as-is)
Safeguard caps	Concurrent enemy/projectile cap = mobile frame defense

Status chains are elemental reactions

BotW's "electricity travels through metal" rule maps straight onto a defense game's "shock chains through
wet/metal enemy crowds." Just read the ReactionRule table as enemy status effects.

// "Shock chains through wet enemies (jumps to neighbors)"
new ReactionRule {
    Trigger = ElementTag.Electric,
    TargetMaterials = "WetEnemy;MetalEnemy",
    Effect = StateEffect.Discharge,   // fires a chain-shock event
    Probability = 0.8f,
};

When the line is too easy (low tension) the director seeds rushes/special mobs to squeeze; when it's
overwhelmed (high) it gives breathing room. "Elemental combos" — luring a shock onto a freeze field the
player laid down — fall out of the same table naturally.

Mobile checkpoints

Combos are the feel. Keep chains like freeze → shock in the rule table to add new combos as data, live.

Wave pacing = the difficulty curve. The director adjusts pressure without you hand-authoring every stage.

Caps = performance. A concurrent enemy/projectile cap keeps frames steady even in late-game swarms.

title: Overview
content:
What Tempo does

Tempo is a system that lets the game create crisis situations on its own. A director quietly
seeds conditions — fire, rain, wind — and the world reaction layer picks them up and lets the
situation grow, the way a fire spreads. You don't have to script every scene by hand; a different
situation emerges every time.

Two games inspired it:

Left 4 Dead — automatically adjusts the intensity (the tempo) of the action.

The Legend of Zelda: BotW — fire, water and electricity react with each other by fixed rules.

Why "Tempo": what this package ultimately does is adjust the game's tension tempo (its rise and fall).

The loop

[Director]  ──seed conditions (fire/rain/wind/lightning)──▶  [World Reaction]
   ▲                                                          │
   │  receives tension back                                   │ computes results (spread/quench/charge)
   │  (player threat + what's happening nearby)               ▼
   └──────────────────  [Tension Model]  ◀── player threat / live events

Every frame the three parts run in the same order: tension → director → world.

Part	Class	Role
World reaction	WorldReaction	Spreads by rules on a grid; updates the list of live events
Director	DirectorBrain	Reads tension, picks a phase, seeds conditions within budget
Tension model	TensionModel	Combines player threat + nearby events into one 0–1 number

Core principles

Split the two roles. The world reaction has no idea the director exists. It only spreads by rules.

The director never spawns enemies. It only seeds conditions (fire, rain, wind, storm clouds upstream).

The director watches one number — tension (0–1): player threat combined with nearby events.

All the numbers live outside the code. Rule tables, thresholds and weights are data a designer edits without code.

title: Safeguards
content:
The world can produce chains even the director didn't expect. A few safeguards keep it in check.

1. Caps

Cap the number / total magnitude of simultaneous events. Past the cap, hold off on lighting new fires
(Trigger actions).

protected virtual int MaxActiveEvents => 48;

// inside PickActions
bool overloaded = world.ActiveEvents.Count >= MaxActiveEvents;
if (overloaded && action.Intent == SeedIntent.Trigger) continue; // skip new fire

WorldReaction.BurningCells also exposes the burning-cell count for a stricter cap.

2. Quench first in the relax phase

In the relax phase only Intent == Calm actions (rain, extinguish) are chosen. The default policy
already behaves this way.

3. Mercy when it goes off underfoot

So a condition the director seeded doesn't kill the player instantly right underfoot, ease off near the
player — reduce the power or delay it a beat. (This is where your damage code applies a distance falloff.)

4. Telegraph it (foreshadowing)

The most important one. Conditions the director seeds must be telegraphed — storm clouds gather,
the wind dries out. Without it the player just thinks "why did I suddenly die?"

DryUpwind → wind picking up and drying (rustling grass, sound).

ChargeStorm → storm clouds gathering first.

IgniteUpwind → a small ember/smoke visible upwind in the distance first.

Read DirectorBrain.CurrentPhase and WorldReaction.ActiveEvents to drive your foreshadowing visuals.

Why it matters: BotW used sleight-of-hand tricks, yet still showed clearly what needed showing.
Ultima Online's autonomous ecology, by contrast, failed because players never noticed it.
Show clearly what needs to be shown.

Checking with debug tools

Use the editor's Tools → Tempo → Debug Window to watch the tension graph, phase, event count and
burning cells live. Wire it up from your game code:

#if UNITY_EDITOR
Achieve.Tempo.Editor.DebugWindow.Bind(_tension, _director, _world);
#endif

Before building, Tools → Tempo → Validate Rules (or the automatic build check) catches missing
materials and conflicting rules in the table.
